p-value-calculator.assumptionNote: The statistic must come from a test whose assumptions are met (normality for z, approximate normality for t). This tool computes the p-value; it does not check assumptions.

faqs.a: A p-value is the probability of seeing a test statistic at least this extreme if the null hypothesis were true. p = 0.05 means: if nothing were really happening, results this extreme would occur 5% of the time by chance alone.

A z-test uses the standard normal distribution and applies when the population standard deviation is known or the sample is large. A t-test uses the t-distribution with degrees of freedom and is the right choice for small samples with estimated standard deviation.
faqs.q: What is the difference between a z-test and a t-test?

faqs.a: One-tailed tests one direction only (is it greater?). Two-tailed tests either direction (is it different?). Two-tailed is the default in most research because it does not assume the direction in advance.

0.05 is the conventional significance level: a p-value below it is called statistically significant. It is a historical convention from the 1920s, not a law of nature - always report the exact p-value too.

No. A p-value measures surprise under the null hypothesis, not the probability that the hypothesis is true, and not the size of the effect. A tiny p-value can come from a trivial effect in a huge sample.
faqs.q: Does a small p-value prove my hypothesis?

faqs.a: The t-distribution has heavier tails than the normal distribution, accounting for the extra uncertainty of estimating the standard deviation from a small sample. As degrees of freedom grow, the t-distribution converges to the normal.
faqs.q: Why do I need degrees of freedom for a t-test?

p-value-calculator.formula:
Z-test: p = 2 x (1 - Phi(|z|)) for two-tailed; p = 1 - Phi(z) for one-tailed.
Phi is the standard normal CDF.
T-test with v degrees of freedom: two-tailed p = I(v/(v+t^2), v/2, 1/2),
where I is the regularized incomplete beta function.
Significant when p < 0.05.
howTo: Enter your test statistic (the z or t value from your analysis).
For t-tests, enter the degrees of freedom.
Read the p-value and the plain-words significance verdict.
keyFacts: The p-value is the probability of results at least this extreme under the null hypothesis.
Smaller p means more surprising results if the null were true.
p < 0.05 is the conventional bar for statistical significance.
Z-tests use the normal distribution; t-tests use the t-distribution with degrees of freedom.
Two-tailed tests check both directions; one-tailed checks one.
A p-value is not the probability that the hypothesis is true.

p-value-calculator.quickAnswer: A z-score of 1.96, two-tailed, gives p = 0.05: there is a 5% chance of seeing results this extreme if nothing were really happening. That is exactly the conventional significance threshold, so the result is significant at the 5% level. This calculator handles z-tests and t-tests, one or two-tailed, and states the verdict in plain words.
p-value-calculator.tagline: P-values from z or t statistics - one or two-tailed, with a clear verdict.
p-value-calculator.workedExample:
Z = 1.96, two-tailed:
1. Standard normal CDF at 1.96: Phi(1.96) = 0.975.
2. Upper tail: 1 - 0.975 = 0.025.
3. Two-tailed: 2 x 0.025 = 0.05.
4. Compare with 0.05: 0.05 is not less than 0.05, so this is right on the boundary - significant at the 5% level by convention (p <= 0.05).
5. T-test version with 10 df and t = 1.96 gives p = 0.0784, not significant - heavier tails need stronger evidence.
